Project Brief version 3

Download the PDF The same Brief as a two-page document.

1. The organization

Fernhill Software is a useful fiction, a business-software firm with about 1,100 engineers in 120 product teams. It hires engineers on technical skill and promotes its strongest into management, where some struggle. In 2025, as AI coding tools arrive, an AI enthusiast on the leadership team proposes a three-part reorganization. First, hire professional managers on people skill instead of promoting engineers. Second, make each team’s engineer-manager its technical lead, keeping technical judgment but managing no one. Third, let AI fill the manager’s technical gaps. Fernhill runs a one-year pilot from July 2025, assigning its 120 teams by lot to three arms of 40 so the reorganization and AI can be told apart. People Operations measures the manager–lead relationship from month one.

2. The model

A team delivers when two jobs get done, coordinating people and resolving technical unknowns. The proposal splits those jobs between a manager and a lead, with AI assisting both. Splitting a job creates a third job, keeping the two roles working together.

  1. People skill lowers coordination friction. Less work sits blocked on other people, more so in bigger teams.
  2. Difficulty sets how many unknowns arrive. AI resolves routine ones but helps little on hard ones.
  3. Escalated unknowns queue at whoever holds technical judgment, the engineer-manager or a tech lead with far more time. Near capacity, the wait explodes (Little’s Law).
  4. Every escalated unknown in the new structure crosses the manager–lead relationship. A weak one adds waiting, rework, and overridden estimates, most on hard work.
  5. The relationship evolves from the pair’s fit, the lead’s lost status, and the manager’s technical grasp (scarce in 2025, when that skill commanded a premium), reshaped by results and by HR.
  6. Weak relationships drive departures, the lead’s above all, and each departure lowers the next quarter’s delivery.
  7. HR can act only on what is measured. It coaches falling pairs and re-pairs those that don’t recover.

In short, the relationship decides whether the new structure works, above all on hard work.

For the model to be right, the relationship score must track the working relationship, not politeness. Teams must stay in their arm, and teams without AI must go without it. Enough leads must exist to make re-pairing possible. Difficulty must be judgeable at quarterly planning. What stays unmeasured is the pair’s fit and the judgment holder’s capacity, seen only through the relationship and the waits.

3. The question

Should Fernhill replace engineer-managers with professional managers backed by technical leads and AI? And does HR’s tending of the manager–lead relationship matter? The pilot answers with three comparisons, with each arm also set against its own eight pre-pilot quarters. The first compares AI, holding structure fixed (engineer-managers with and without AI). The second compares structure, holding AI fixed (manager + lead vs. engineer-manager, both with AI), the decision Fernhill faces. The third compares HR’s response (within manager + lead, HR acting vs. scores sealed), to see whether tending the relationship helps.

4. The prediction

Stated before looking at this version’s data:

  • AI alone behaves as in version 2, better on easy quarters and flat on hard ones.
  • The relationship score predicts delivery more strongly in the new structure than under engineer-managers, and on hard quarters than easy ones.
  • The new structure on hard quarters splits by the relationship. Strong pairs match or beat engineer-managers with AI, and weak pairs fall well behind.
  • Lead departures concentrate in pairs whose score fell in the first two quarters.
  • Where HR acts, fewer pairs stay weak and fewer leads leave, but a year may be too short to show delivery gains.

The model is wrong if any of these holds:

  • The relationship score predicts nothing beyond the escalation load.
  • Weak and strong pairs deliver about the same on hard quarters.
  • HR raises the scores but not delivery or retention. Then it improves the measure, not the work.

5. The data sketch

The data. Fernhill’s records have one row per team per quarter, July 2023 to June 2026 (1,440 rows), and they are simulated, since Fernhill is fictional. The variables, by concept. The change is arm and HR’s lot, manager type, and AI licenses, with IT’s usage logs. The manager has a people-skill rating on the eight Project Oxygen behaviors, the hours work sits blocked on other teams, and a technical score at hire. The work has team size, and difficulty rated at planning and again at close. Unknowns are escalations, the hours each waits, and escalations open at close. The relationship has a monthly relational-coordination pulse in every arm, overrides of the lead’s estimates, and the lead’s former role. HR and people have coaching, re-pairing, and departures. The outcome is the share of committed milestones delivered on time.

6. The disciplinary anchor

Whom to promote (organizational management). Firms promote their best performers, who then make worse managers (Peter and Hull, 1969; Benson, Li and Shue, 2019). People skill keeps teams together (Hoffman and Tadelis, 2021; Garvin, 2013), but so do a boss’s technical competence and the prize of promotion (Artz, Goodall and Oswald, 2017; Lazear and Rosen, 1981).

The work itself (operations management). Unknowns go up the hierarchy unless knowledge is cheap, and AI makes only routine knowledge cheap (Galbraith, 1974; Garicano, 2000; Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, 2025; METR, 2025). Waits grow when escalations arrive faster than they are cleared (Little’s Law), and firefighting slows recovery (Repenning and Sterman, 2001).

The bridge and the method. Split roles must be integrated (Lawrence and Lorsch, 1967), and relational coordination matters more as uncertainty rises (Gittell, 2002). The method follows Pearl (2019). The relationship enters only because the diagram, drawn before the data, demands it.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) to diagram how an escalated unknown gets resolved and to find a relationship measure. I added an override count to the relational-coordination survey it suggested, since a score that decides coaching gets gamed. I also chose a second lot over its idea of HR acting on every low score, since low scores rise on their own.

Data & Methods draft version 3

Download the PDF The same draft as a two-page document, with its charts.

The data behind every number here: fernhill_v3.csv, also in The data below.

1. Unit of observation

One row of my main file is one product team in one quarter, because the lot assigns whole teams and delivery is counted by the quarter. The relationship belongs to a pair, a manager and a lead, so each row also carries a pair ID. There are 1,440 rows, from 120 teams over 12 quarters, July 2023 to June 2026, eight before the pilot and four during it. A pair changes when a lead leaves or HR re-pairs (a mid-quarter change is recorded as the quarter’s pair), so the teams hold 219 pairs in all. The lot assigned teams, 40 to each of three arms (engineer-managers without and with AI, and a manager and lead with AI), so arm comparisons rest on 40 teams each, not on 480 team-quarters. A second lot, inside the new structure, assigned HR’s response, 20 teams HR acts on and 20 sealed. A second file holds the monthly pulses, one row per pair per pilot month (1,440 rows). It joins on pair ID and quarter together, since on pair ID alone a pair matches all of its months, and 480 team-quarters become 5,250 rows.

2. Variable table

Concept Variable Kind Source What it misses
Structure, AI and HR’s lot arm, hr_acts Labels, yes/no Pilot register Drift from the arm
Relationship rc_score, overrides Measurement (index), count Pulse survey, audit log Politeness, and gaming once HR acts on it
Difficulty hard_plan Yes/No Planning review Misjudged quarters
Waiting esc_wait_hrs Measurement (hours) Tracker Untracked waits
Departures lead_departed Yes/No HR system Leads who checked out but stayed
Delivery delivered_share Measurement (share) Planning tool Customer value and renegotiation

3. Data source

Fernhill’s pilot register, People Operations’ pulse survey and pair register, the planning tool and its audit log, the issue tracker, the planning review, and the HR system, read through People Analytics, cover all 120 teams for all 12 quarters. The pulse and the overrides begin in July 2025, since People Operations measured the relationship from month one, in every arm. I use the overrides, a behavior and not an answer, only to check the score. Fernhill is a useful fiction, so these records are simulated. These data are simulated from the model described above. Its assumptions, written down before the data were generated, are that teams are independent, the lots hold, and AI is truly withheld from the no-AI arm. The relationship rests on the pair’s unobserved fit, the managers’ skills, and the lead’s lost status, and responds to coaching. AI clears routine escalations more than hard ones, and escalations queue at whoever holds technical judgment. A firm-wide migration lowers delivery for every team from July 2025. The score can be gamed once HR acts on it, and overrides cannot. Every measure carries random noise.

4. Quality concern

The relationship score is the most likely to mislead, being a survey index and the one number HR now acts on. It is mismeasured where people answer politely, and where HR acts on it, since pairs can learn to score higher without working better (Goodhart’s law). It is missing for 71 of 1,440 pulses (5%). If so, I would see scores in the teams HR acts on sitting above what their overrides imply, while sealed teams’ scores track them. I will report the blanks and never fill them in, average each quarter’s answered months (68 of 480 scores rest on one or two pulses), read the score beside the overrides, and compare teams HR acts on with sealed teams, since the lot decides who is coached.

5. First description

Delivery (delivered_share). Kind: a measurement, a share from 0 to 1. How many: 1,440, none blank. Middle, spread and shape: median 0.68, and mean 0.64, which a tail of bad quarters pulls down. Half fall between 0.50 and 0.82, the range is 0 to 1, and the shape is skewed left, with 19 under 5%. Choice: each team-quarter counts once, whatever its size. Weighting by milestones gives 0.64.

Against my model: not yet able to say, since one variable can’t show whether the arms differ.

Relationship (rc_score). Kind: a measurement, an index built from ordered labels (the mean of seven 1 to 5 items, averaged over a quarter’s pulses). How many: 480, all in the pilot, with 960 blank before July 2025. The 1,440 monthly pulses have 71 blank (5%), from 53 teams, at most 4 each. Middle, spread and shape: median 3.4, and mean 3.41. Half fall between 2.9 and 3.9, the range is 1.3 to 5.0, and the shape is roughly symmetric, with 30 pulses at the 1 or 5 limits. The monthly average barely moves (3.3 to 3.4), but single pairs wander: in 50 teams the last three months sit at least 0.5 from the first three (the chart shows 40 teams at random). Choice: blanks left out. A mean of ordered items assumes equal steps, so I checked it against the median (3.4), nearly the same.

Against my model: not yet able to say, since the score tracking delivery takes two variables.

Waiting (esc_wait_hrs). Kind: a measurement, in hours. How many: 1,399, with 41 blank (3%), in the tracker. Middle, spread and shape: median 15.3 hours, and mean 26.4, which a few long waits pull up (23 over 100 hours, kept), so I report the median. Half fall between 8.4 and 34.5 hours, and the range is 3.2 to 759.3. Against my model: not yet able to say. A long right tail is what any queue produces, and one variable can’t show whether the structure changes it.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) for the counts, middles, spreads, and histograms. I checked its mean of the score against the median, and rejected its offer to fill the blank pulses, since a filled-in month is a pulse nobody took.

Work it yourself: the Data & Methods prompts version 3

These are the prompts for the Data & Methods draft above, in order. Download fernhill_v3.csv and fernhill_v3_pulse.csv, start a new Gemini chat with your Willamette account, upload both files, and paste each prompt into the same chat. (The Results prompts that follow continue in the same chat, and the usage file, fernhill_ai_usage.csv, goes in before P18.) Think about the question before you open “What we found.” Gemini’s wording and charts will differ from ours, but the numbers should match. If a number doesn’t, that’s a check worth running.

What is new since version 2. There are now two files, and joining them is the first trap. The model has a box nobody measured in versions 1 and 2, the relationship between manager and lead, and a score for it that HR acts on, so the question is no longer only whether a column is right but whether a number that decides something can still be believed. Every number below was recomputed from the files, and we ran all twenty prompts in one Gemini chat (the link is below). Where Gemini’s answer differed from ours, or added something we did not ask for, a line beginning “In our run” says so.

See exactly how we ran it Gemini's answers to these prompts, step by step (the shared chat, which opens when you sign in with your Willamette account).

P1

What is a row, and what is compared?

What does one row of fernhill_v3.csv represent? How many rows are there, how many different teams do they cover, how many quarters, and how many teams are in each arm? Within the arm ML_AI, how many teams does hr_acts mark yes and how many no? How many different pair_id values are there, and why are there more of them than teams?

The lot assigned teams, and a second lot assigned HR's response. How many independent units does each comparison really have, and what is a pair?

What we found

One row is one product team in one quarter, with 1,440 rows, 120 teams and 12 quarters (2023Q3 to 2026Q2), eight before the pilot and four during it. Each arm has 40 teams, and inside the new structure (ML_AI) HR acts on 20 teams and 20 stay sealed. There are 219 different pair IDs, more than the 120 teams, because a pair changes when a lead leaves or HR re-pairs the manager, so some teams hold two, three or more pairs over the three years. Arm comparisons rest on 40 teams a side, and the HR comparison on 20. hr_acts is blank outside the new structure, and rc_score and overrides exist only from July 2025.

In our run Gemini named the unit a team-quarter, gave every count correctly, and explained the 219 pair IDs by counting the three ways a pair changes (a lead leaves, the pilot brings a professional manager, a manager is re-paired).

P2

Describe the outcome

Describe delivered_share: what kind of variable it is, how many values there are including blanks, the middle (the median, and the mean only if a mean makes sense for this kind of variable), how spread out it is, and its shape, with a histogram in five-point bands. Tell me any choices you made, such as dropping blanks or zeros, and whether each team-quarter counts once or is weighted.

Which is larger, the mean or the median? Why?

What we found
Question Answer
Kind A measurement, a share from 0 to 1
How many 1,440, none blank
Middle Median 0.68, and mean 0.64
Spread Half fall between 0.50 and 0.82, and the range is 0 to 1
Shape Skewed left, with a long tail of quarters that delivered little (19 are under 5%)

The mean sits below the median because of that tail. A choice worth naming. Each team-quarter counts once, whatever its size, and weighting by milestones gives 0.64.

P3

Describe the score, and its monthly path

Describe rc_score the same way. It is the mean of seven 1 to 5 relationship items, averaged over a quarter's monthly pulses, and it is blank before July 2025. Tell me how many values are present and blank. Then, using fernhill_v3_pulse.csv, tell me how many monthly pulses are blank and in how many teams, how many sit at exactly 1 or 5, and how the average pulse moves from month to month. For how many teams do the last three months average at least 0.5 away from the first three?

A score built from ordered answers is averaged. Is the mean the right summary, and what would you check it against? What would a flat monthly average hide?

What we found
Question Answer
Kind A measurement, an index built from ordered labels
How many 480, all in the pilot, with 960 blank before July 2025 (when nobody measured it)
Middle Median 3.4, and mean 3.41
Spread Half fall between 2.9 and 3.9, and the range is 1.3 to 5.0
Shape Roughly symmetric

The monthly file has 1,440 pulses, 71 blank (5%) from 53 teams, at most 4 each, and 30 at the 1 or 5 limits. The average pulse barely moves (3.3 to 3.4 across the twelve months), but single pairs wander: in 50 of the 120 teams the last three months average at least 0.5 from the first three. A flat average can hide a lot of movement underneath it. The mean of ordered items assumes equal steps between answers, which is a choice to defend, and the median (3.4) is nearly the same, so here the choice changes little. Leave the blank pulses blank.

In our run Gemini gave every number correctly and left the blank pulses blank. Unasked, it split the monthly average by arm, which shows the new structure’s score rising from about 3.0 to 3.4 while the other two arms drift. That is the first hint that the flat average hides something.

P4

Join the files, and check the lots

Join the pulse file to the pilot-quarter rows of fernhill_v3.csv on pair_id and quarter together, and tell me how many rows result. Then join on pair_id alone and tell me how many rows result and why the number is different. Last, for the 40 teams in ML_AI, compare hr_acts yes with no on the average delivered_share before the pilot, and on the average rc_score in 2025Q3, the first pilot quarter.

Each team-quarter has three months of pulses. What should a join on a pair that lasts several quarters do? If the lot is fair, how alike should the two HR groups be before anything happens?

What we found

Joined on pair_id and quarter, the 480 pilot team-quarters give 1,440 rows (three months each). Joined on pair_id alone they give 5,250, because a pair that lasts several quarters matches all of its months, not only the quarter’s three. Before the join, decide what one row of the result should be. For the two HR groups, delivery before the pilot is alike (67.0% for the 20 teams HR acts on and 67.8% for the 20 sealed), but the first pilot quarter’s score is not (2.90 against 3.06). A lot is fair in expectation and can still be uneven with 20 teams a side, and this one gave the HR group weaker pairs to start with (13 of 20 under 3.0 against 8, a difference chance reaches about one time in five).

In our run Gemini explained the 5,250 as a many-to-many join within each pair and tabulated it by how many quarters a pair lasts. Unasked, it ran two t-tests on the HR groups (p = 0.83 and p = 0.22). Both readings were fair, and neither is something this prompt asks for.

P5

Where could the score mislead you?

My data is Fernhill Software's records, one row per product team per quarter. For each of these, say whether it could affect my data and what I would see in the data if it were happening: missing values, mismeasurement, a definition that changed, only some cases recorded, dates or entries shifted. Focus on rc_score, which HR acts on in the 20 ML_AI teams with hr_acts = yes. Then give the average rc_score and the average overrides by quarter, separately for hr_acts yes and no, in ML_AI.

A score that decides something can be worked on. What would you see in the score and in the overrides if pairs learned to score well, and which of the two is harder to game?

What we found
Average by quarter 2025Q3 2025Q4 2026Q1 2026Q2
Score, HR acts 2.90 3.14 3.24 3.40
Score, sealed 3.06 3.11 3.19 3.28
Overrides, HR acts 2.35 2.75 1.90 2.65
Overrides, sealed 2.10 2.25 2.15 1.75

Several of the five apply to rc_score. It is missing for 960 rows and for 5% of its monthly pulses. It is mismeasured wherever people answer politely, and where HR acts on it, since once a score decides coaching, pairs can learn to score higher without working better (Goodhart’s law). The score rose faster where HR acts (up 0.50, against 0.22), but overrides did not fall there (2.65 in the last quarter, against 1.75 for sealed teams). An override is a behavior, so it is harder to game than an answer. The draft picks one concern, says what it would see (HR-acts scores sitting above what the overrides imply) and what it will do (read the score beside the overrides, and compare against the sealed teams).

In our run Gemini gave every quarterly average correctly and named four of the five concerns with what each would look like. It described HR’s rule as strict, coaching whenever a score falls below 3.0, but in the data only 17 of the 24 low scores were followed by coaching. Check a rule it states in general terms.

P6

Hold it up against the prediction

My model predicts that the relationship score tracks delivery more in the new structure and on hard quarters, that the new structure's hard quarters split by the relationship, and that where HR acts fewer pairs stay weak and fewer leads leave. Based only on the descriptions above, does the data look the way the model says it should? What can a description of one variable at a time not tell me?

What would you write for each of the three predictions, using only what you have described so far?

What we found

From the descriptions alone, not yet able to say, for all three. Each description is of one variable at a time, and none can show how the score relates to delivery, whether hard quarters split, or what HR’s response did. Gemini may not stop there. Asked to use only the descriptions, it may go back to the file and compare groups itself, which is the Results draft arriving early. Read any verdict it gives against what the Results prompts find, and notice any “significantly” with no test behind it, any causal verb (“HR raised the scores”), and any average of the score that ignores the lot.

In our run Gemini stayed with the descriptions. It said it could not tell for three of the four predictions and called the fourth partly consistent but inconclusive. It named regression to the mean and selection as things a one-variable description cannot rule out.

Results draft version 3

Download the PDF The same draft as a two-page document, with its charts.

The data behind every number here: fernhill_v3.csv, also in The data below.

1. The question and the prediction

My question is causal, in two parts. Does the relationship between a team’s manager and its lead decide whether the new structure works, above all on hard work, and does HR’s tending of it matter? Delivery is the share of a team’s committed milestones delivered by their dates. The two lots, one for the arms and one for HR’s response, would let me call those differences effects, but nobody assigned the relationship, so what I say about it is an association, and this draft leaves the causal claim for Module 3. My model predicts that the relationship score tracks delivery more in the new structure and on hard quarters, that the new structure’s hard quarters split by it, with strong pairs matching engineer-managers with AI and weak pairs well behind, that lead departures follow weak pairs, and that where HR acts fewer pairs stay weak and fewer leads leave, though a year may be too short to show delivery gains.

2. The charts

This chart answers: how do hard quarters deliver in each arm, and, in the new structure, by the relationship score?

Delivery is a measurement (a share), the arm is a label, and the score is an index of ordered labels, split into thirds within the new structure at 2.9 and 3.5. Each dot is a group’s average over its pilot hard quarters, with their count in brackets.

This chart answers: where HR acts on the score, do the teams differ from sealed ones, and does the score show it?

Each pair of dots compares 20 teams HR acts on with 20 whose scores stay sealed. Delivery and the share rated hard at planning are shares, the score is an index, and overrides are counts a team’s manager made.

3. The association

AI alone is version 2’s result, to the decimal (10.7 points on easy quarters and 9.5 on hard, raw),

The relationship splits the new structure’s hard quarters. They delivered 33.0% in the weakest third of the score, 55.4% in the middle, and 63.5% in the strongest, against 55.3% under engineer-managers with AI. The 74 quarters come from 35 teams, 16 to 19 a third, and resampling whole teams puts the strongest-against-weakest gap (30.5 points) between 16 and 44. Halves give 39.1% and 62.2%. The score tracks delivery most on hard quarters in the new structure (correlation 0.49, against 0.34 on easy ones), but just as well on hard quarters under engineer-managers without AI (0.49), so “more in the new structure” only half holds. Leads left in 15.3% of team-quarters in the weak third, 4.8% in the middle and none in the strongest (same cuts, all 160 team-quarters), though a fall in the score over the first two quarters marked them less well (5 of 14 teams, against 7 of 26).

HR’s response can’t be read from 20 teams a side. Teams HR acts on delivered 60.3% in the pilot against 67.4% for sealed teams, after delivering alike before it (67.0% and 67.8%). The lot also gave them more hard quarters (50.0% rated hard at planning, against 42.5%) and weaker pairs (13 of 20 scored under 3.0 in the first quarter, against 8). By difficulty the gap is 2.0 points on hard quarters and 8.1 on easy ones. Fewer pairs were still under 3.0 at the end where HR acts (3 against 7), and fewer leads left (5.0% a quarter against 10.0%). The score rose more there (2.90 to 3.40, against 3.06 to 3.28) while overrides did not fall (2.65 in the last quarter, against 1.75). But none of this stands out from chance. Shuffling the HR labels among the 40 teams reaches a delivery gap this large (7.2 points by team) about one time in five, the score’s rise one time in eight, and last-quarter overrides one in six.

AI use is chosen, not assigned. Among licensed teams, heavy users (at or above the median use) delivered 65.5% and light users 65.1%, as if use did nothing, but on easy quarters heavy users delivered 78.5% against 73.3%, on hard ones 52.3% against 53.0%, and heavy users drew more hard quarters (49.7% against 40.3%), which hides the easy-quarter gain in the pooled figure.

4. Against the model

The Brief named three ways the model would be wrong. The score predicts delivery beyond the escalation load (about 24 points per point of score on hard quarters in the new structure, with or without the load held fixed), so the first doesn’t hold. Weak and strong pairs deliver 33.0% and 63.5% on hard quarters, so the second doesn’t hold. The third I can’t judge. Where HR acts the score rose and leads stayed, but delivery was no better, overrides did not fall, and none of it is outside chance.

5. What this does not establish

Nobody assigned the relationship. Results feed back, so last quarter’s delivery predicts this quarter’s score (correlation 0.30) about as well as last quarter’s score predicts delivery (0.34), and the thirds sort quarters by a score measured in the same quarter as the delivery. A team’s capability, which no column holds, can move both. Across all pilot teams the slope falls from 12.4 to 8.5 points per point of score once each team’s own before-period delivery is held fixed, though not in the new structure alone (17.8 to 18.1). That is an association.

The lot for HR’s response is too small to tell. Difficulty rated at planning is the right adjustment, since it was set before the work, but it doesn’t close the gap on easy quarters, and none is outside chance.

My Data & Methods concern, the score gamed once HR acts on it, would show as scores rising where overrides don’t, and a little does, though within chance. The two groups’ scores averaged alike (3.17 and 3.16) while overrides ran higher where HR acts (2.41 against 2.06).

What would settle it is the Interpretation in Module 3: which rung each comparison reaches, what coaching pairs by lot would add, and a forecast with a range for the decision.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) for the comparisons, the thirds, and the charts. It compared HR’s teams with sealed ones on delivery alone, and I added the lot’s hard quarters, first-quarter scores and overrides. It pooled heavy and light users, and I split them by difficulty.

Work it yourself: the Results prompts version 3

These are the prompts for the Results draft above, in order, in the same chat as the Data & Methods prompts (or a new one with fernhill_v3.csv and fernhill_v3_pulse.csv uploaded again, and fernhill_ai_usage.csv before P18). Think about the question before you open “What we found.” Gemini’s charts and wording will differ from ours, but the numbers should match. If a number doesn’t, that’s a check worth running.

This model is the biggest yet. Two lots, a relationship nobody assigned, a score that can be gamed and a usage record chosen by teams make a dozen analyses in a two-page draft, so the prompts ask for every number the draft needs and say exactly what each chart must show. Three habits recur. Split by hard_plan, rated at planning, never hard_close, rated after the outcome. Say what one dot is. And separate what a lot lets you claim (the arms, and HR’s response) from what nobody assigned (the relationship, and AI use). We ran all twenty prompts in one Gemini chat, and where its answer differed from ours, or added something we did not ask for, a line beginning “In our run” says so.

See exactly how we ran it Gemini's answers to these prompts, step by step (the shared chat, which opens when you sign in with your Willamette account).

P7

Where the arms stand

What does this not establish?

In ML_AI, compute the correlation between rc_score in a quarter and delivered_share in the previous quarter, and between delivered_share in a quarter and rc_score in the previous quarter, for quarters 2025Q4 to 2026Q2. Then, for all pilot team-quarters with a score, give the slope of delivered_share on rc_score in points per point of score, first alone and then with each team's average delivered_share over the eight pre quarters held fixed, and do the same for ML_AI alone.

The model says results feed back into the relationship, and that team capability could drive both. What would each of those look like in these numbers?

What we found

Last quarter’s score predicts this quarter’s delivery (0.34) about as well as last quarter’s delivery predicts this quarter’s score (0.30), on 120 team-quarters. A good quarter sours or sweetens the pair, so the arrow runs both ways. For the slope, across all pilot teams it falls from 12.4 to 8.5 points per point of score once each team’s own before-period delivery is held fixed, but in the new structure alone it barely moves (17.8 and 18.1). Part of the link across arms is team capability, which moves both, and nothing in this file holds it directly. All of this is an association, the first rung, and it is why the draft leaves the causal claim for Module 3.

In our run Gemini labelled the two lagged correlations correctly (0.34 and 0.30) and gave both sets of slopes. It added p-values and the words “statistically significant” unasked, and it did not read the lagged correlations as causal.

How firm is the split by relationship?

What we found

The 74 quarters come from 35 teams, with 16, 19 and 16 teams in the weak, middle and strong thirds. The strongest third delivers 30.5 points more than the weakest, and resampling whole teams puts that gap between about 16 and 44 points. Halves of the score give 39.1% and 62.2%, so the gradient doesn’t depend on the cut. This is the split the draft rests on, and it is firm in a way the HR comparisons are not. It remains an association, because nobody assigned the relationship.

In our run Gemini resampled whole teams, found 16, 19 and 16 teams in the three thirds, and gave a middle 95% of 14.9 to 43.6 points around the 30.5 gap. Your interval will differ by a point or two, since the resamples are random. The halves of the score gave 39.1% and 62.2%.

Interpretation version 3

1. My causal claim

Giving AI to teams run by engineer-managers raised their delivery. With each team set against its own eight quarters before the pilot, the lot puts the gain at 4.3 points (a 90% range of about 0 to 9), on easy quarters (4.2) and hard ones (3.1) alike. Replacing engineer-managers with a professional manager and a technical lead, both with AI, did not raise delivery on average. The new structure delivered 3.4 points less than engineer-managers with AI (about −10 to 3), 3.4 less on hard quarters and 1.4 more on easy ones, and its teams spread much further apart. The person holding technical judgment left more often in the new structure, a lead in 12 of 160 team-quarters against the most senior engineer in 5 of 160 under engineer-managers with AI (shuffling the arm labels across teams reaches that gap about one time in twenty). Within the new structure, pairs with a strong relationship delivered well on hard work and weak pairs badly, but nobody assigned the relationship, so that part is an association. Whether HR’s tending of the relationship helps, this year cannot say.

2. My causal diagram

The lot set who got which structure and AI, so no back door reaches the arm comparisons. The relationship sits on the path from the new structure to delivery, since every escalated unknown crosses it, and the escalation wait is the step I can measure. On the new structure’s hard quarters the median wait was 61.2 hours in the weakest third of the score, 27.2 in the middle and 13.3 in the strongest, against 27.8 under engineer-managers with AI. The rival I took most seriously is the team’s own capability, which no column holds. A capable team builds a good relationship and also delivers, and its delivery feeds back into the score. That back door stays open. Holding each team’s delivery before the pilot fixed closes part of it across all teams (the slope falls from 12.4 to 8.5 points per point of score), but not in the new structure alone (17.8 to 18.1), so I can’t close it with these data.

3. The rung my evidence reaches

The arm comparisons reach doing, the second rung. The lot is an experiment, and setting each team against its own before-period makes it a comparison of changes inside one. Forty teams a side keep the ranges wide, so I am fairly sure of AI’s direction and not of its size, and the structure’s net effect could have either sign. The relationship reaches seeing, the first rung. It is well measured from the first month, and the waits fall where the model says they should, but nobody assigned it. HR’s response was designed to reach doing, but 20 teams a side cannot speak, as the Results draft found (a shuffle reaches its gap about one time in five). Imagining, what a given team would have delivered with a different lead, is out of reach.

What I tried. For this section I compared the arms twelve ways, AI and the structure, raw and against each team’s before-period, over all quarters, easy ones and hard ones, and I added the lead departures and the waits by third, fourteen comparisons in all. I report the before-period version of every arm comparison, whichever way it moved the number, because the lot left AI’s two arms apart before the pilot (61.5% against 66.9%). Raw, AI’s gain is 9.7 points, about twice what I report. The relationship’s cut is the Results draft’s thirds, and halves tell the same story (39.1% against 62.2%).

4. What it would take to know more

The next rung for the relationship is to assign what builds it. Fernhill can’t assign how well two people work together, but it can assign coaching and re-pairing by lot, which is what HR’s lot tried on 20 teams a side. With the spread of this year’s team changes (20.3 points), seeing a 5-point gain in delivery with fair confidence would take about 260 teams a side, more teams than Fernhill has. So the affordable step is to measure the step the effect runs through. The score, the overrides, the waits and lead departures all move within a quarter or two, and they can be read on every new pair from its first month, with coaching assigned by lot. Is it worth it? Moving all 120 teams to the new structure is costly to undo, since leads who lose a manager’s role leave, and the evidence allows a loss of 10 points. Waiting costs little, because AI can go to the engineer-managers’ teams now. So more information is worth buying before restructuring, and not before giving AI.

5. My forecast for the decision

I recommend giving AI to every engineer-manager’s team now, and growing the new structure only as an experiment.

If Fernhill gives AI to all its engineer-managers’ teams, I expect delivery between about 0 and 9 points higher over the next year than without it, most likely about 4, or up to about 870 more of the roughly 9,700 milestones a year’s teams commit (about 420 most likely). This assumes the gain travels from the 40 pilot teams to the other 80, the licensed tools stay as they are, and the 2025 customer migration was a one-off shared by every team.

If instead Fernhill moved all 120 teams to the new structure, I expect delivery between about 10 points lower and 3 points higher than engineer-managers with AI, most likely about 3 lower (about 970 fewer to 290 more milestones a year), with more teams far from the average and more leads leaving. This assumes the professional managers hired for 120 teams are as good as the 40 hired for the pilot, enough leads stay to fill the role, and about 44% of quarters stay hard. A thinner pool of managers at scale would move this range down, not up.

For whom or when might it not hold? The new structure’s range is widest on hard work, where weak pairs delivered 33.0% and strong ones 63.5%, so teams with mostly hard work and newly formed pairs are where it is most likely to fail, and teams with mostly easy work are where it might help (1.4 points, about −5 to 7). The Brief named difficulty before looking, since the model says unknowns arrive with hard work. The relationship I can only describe, so I don’t forecast by it.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) for every comparison above, with the prompts below (P21 to P25), and checked its numbers against the course’s script. It computed the ranges in P21 from a formula instead of resampling, which it disclosed, and they agree with resampling within a few tenths. I added the two caveats it left out, that the departures compare a lead with a senior engineer and that turning points into milestones assumes next year looks like this one. It claimed no cause from the relationship, and I kept it that way.

Work it yourself: the Interpretation prompts version 3

These are the prompts for the Interpretation above, in the same chat as the Results prompts (or a new one with fernhill_v3.csv uploaded again). Think about the question before you open “What we found.” Gemini’s wording will differ from ours, but the numbers should match, apart from the ranges, which come from random resampling and move by a few tenths from run to run.

We ran all five on Thu Nov 19 in a fresh chat on Gemini 4 Hydrogen Thinking, with fernhill_v3.csv attached. Every number matched the course’s script. The notes after each step say where Gemini took a different road or left out a caveat you should add.

Two habits carry over from the Results prompts. Compare teams, not team-quarters, since the lot assigned teams. And set each team against its own eight quarters before the pilot, as we did for SmartShift, because the lot can leave arms unequal by chance.

See exactly how we ran it Gemini's answers to these prompts, step by step (the shared chat, which opens when you sign in with your Willamette account).

P21

Each arm against its own before-period

For each of the 120 teams in fernhill_v3.csv, compute its average delivered_share over the eight pre quarters and over the four pilot quarters, and the change (pilot minus pre), in percentage points. Then compare arms by their teams' average change, EM_AI minus EM_noAI (the AI comparison) and ML_AI minus EM_AI (the structure comparison). Do the same using only the pilot quarters rated hard at planning (hard_plan = yes), and only the easy ones, still against each team's whole before-period. For each of the six comparisons, resample whole teams within each arm 10,000 times and give the middle 90% of the difference. Also give each arm's average before the pilot, the raw pilot gap for AI with no before-period, and the standard deviation of the teams' changes in ML_AI and EM_AI.

The lot assigned teams to arms, so why set each team against its own past at all? Look at the arms before the pilot before you decide.

What we found
Comparison, against each team’s before-period All quarters Easy quarters Hard quarters
AI (EM_AI minus EM_noAI) 4.3 (about 0 to 9) 4.2 (about −1 to 9) 3.1 (about −3 to 10)
Structure (ML_AI minus EM_AI) −3.4 (about −10 to 3) 1.4 (about −5 to 7) −3.4 (about −11 to 4)

The lot left AI’s two arms apart before the pilot, 61.5% (EM_noAI) against 66.9% (EM_AI), with ML_AI at 67.4%. Raw, AI’s pilot gap is 9.7 points by team, about twice the 4.3 that remains once each team is set against its own past. The structure’s ranges cross zero everywhere, and its teams spread far more (a standard deviation of 20.3 points in the new structure against 12.7 under engineer-managers with AI). The hard and easy comparisons rest on 35 and 38 to 39 teams an arm, the teams that had such quarters.

In our run Gemini gave every average, both spreads (20.34 and 12.75) and the raw gap (9.69) correctly, and noticed on its own that more than half of the raw gap was there before the pilot. It did not resample. It said it had reached its limit for running code and computed the ranges from a formula instead, and said so in a note, which is the right thing to do. Its ranges land within a few tenths of ours (for example about −0.4 to 8.9 for AI, against our 0 to 9). If yours resamples, it will differ by a few tenths too. If it neither resamples nor says what it did instead, ask.

P24

What would it take to assign it?

In ML_AI, take each team's change in delivered_share (pilot minus its own pre average, in percentage points) and give its standard deviation. Using the rule of thumb that a comparison of two groups of n teams each sees a gap of d points with about 80% power when n is 2 × (2.8 × sd / d) squared, how many teams a side would a lot need to see a 5-point gain in delivery from coaching? How does that compare with the number of teams Fernhill has?

HR's lot had 20 teams a side. What did that buy, and what would a fair test cost?

What we found

The standard deviation is 20.3 points, so a 5-point gain needs about 260 teams a side, more than Fernhill’s 120 teams in all. That is why the Interpretation turns to the step the effect runs through, the score, overrides, waits and departures, which move faster and can be read on every new pair.

In our run Gemini gave 20.34 and about 260 teams a side (259.5 before rounding up), against Fernhill’s 120 in all and HR’s 20 a side. It also gave a slightly smaller answer, 254, from a second way of computing the spread. Either way the conclusion is the same.

P25

The forecast in milestones

Sum milestones_committed over the 480 pilot team-quarters. Then turn the AI comparison (4.3 points, about 0 to 9) and the structure comparison (−3.4 points, about −10 to 3) into milestones a year at that scale, and give the share of pilot quarters rated hard at planning.

A decision-maker counts milestones, not percentage points. Which assumptions does turning one into the other add?

What we found

The pilot year committed 9,701 milestones. AI’s 4.3 points is about 420 more delivered on time a year (0 to about 870), and the structure’s −3.4 is about 330 fewer (about 970 fewer to 290 more). Of the pilot quarters, 43.8% were rated hard at planning. Turning points into milestones assumes the firm keeps committing about as many, and that the next year’s mix of hard work looks like this one’s.

In our run Gemini gave 9,701, the 43.75% of quarters rated hard, and about 417 and 330 milestones (0 to 873, and 970 fewer to 291 more). It did not say what the conversion assumes, which is the THINK question’s answer and belongs in your forecast sentence.

Three diagrams, one firm version 3

Every version of Fernhill’s analysis rests on a diagram, whether or not anyone drew it. The enthusiast never drew one, so the first drawing is reconstructed from what its file collects and what it compares. The trial designer drew the second, and the gold standard drew the third.

Each box names a concept and, in small type, the column of that firm’s file that records it. A box with no column is a box the firm never measured. Draw yours before you look at the data, because the data can never supply a box nobody drew.

The enthusiast’s diagram

One path from the reorganization to delivery, through people skill, and AI covering the manager’s technical gap. There is no time, no comparison group, and no place for where a technical question goes. The file holds escalations, waits and lead departures, but the diagram gives no reason to look at them.

The trial designer’s diagram

A lot sets who gets which structure and AI, escalations queue into a wait, and delivery follows, moderated by how hard the quarter is. It can say what the arms do. It cannot say why the new structure fails on hard work, because the box where a manager and a lead must agree is not there.

The gold standard’s diagram

The relationship enters because drawing how an escalated unknown actually gets resolved in the new structure forces a box between the manager and the lead. Their traits and the pair’s fit shape it, every escalation crosses it, results and HR reshape it, and weak ones drive leads out. Two things follow that students are meant to find. Good teams build good relationships, so the score tracks delivery even where the relationship matters little, because delivery feeds back into it. And a manager’s people skill drives both the relationship and blocked work, so the score can look like it causes delivery when a common cause is at work.

This drawing is a deliberate simplification. It leaves out team size, the judgment holder’s capacity and the backlog, the 2025 customer migration, each team’s latent capability, and the two readings of difficulty, though the file records some of them.

Notice what the weaker firms hold but never use. The enthusiast’s file has escalations, waits and lead departures, and the trial designer’s has open escalations and lead departures. The columns are there, and the models give no reason to look.
